positions/byzantine-iconoclasm/oneLine: Religious images of Christ and the saints are idols forbidden by the second commandment; the only true image of Christ is the Eucharist, and the saints are honoured by imitating their virtues.
positions/byzantine-iconoclasm/coreClaim: God forbade graven images in worship (Exodus 20:4–5; Deuteronomy 4:15–18).
Christ cannot be depicted without either separating his humanity from his divinity (Nestorianism) or circumscribing the uncircumscribable divinity (Monophysitism).
The Eucharist is the true, God-given image of Christ.
The saints are living images to be imitated, not painted.
positions/byzantine-iconoclasm/origin: Emperor Leo III's measures (traditionally 726/730), possibly in a context of military disasters, volcanic eruption and Islamic aniconism (debated); theological case by Emperor Constantine V (Peuseis) and the Council of Hieria (754); first period ended by Empress Irene at Nicaea II (787); second period 815–843 under Leo V and Theophilus.
positions/byzantine-iconoclasm/strongest: It takes the second commandment seriously.
Its Christological argument exposed a real difficulty: what exactly does an icon of Christ depict?
It sought to purify popular piety from superstition.
John of Damascus: the incarnation makes Christ depictable; refusing images denies his humanity.
God commanded images in the tabernacle and temple.
Iconoclasts persecuted monks and destroyed sacred art and relics.
Its theology was condemned by Nicaea II (787), received by both Rome and Constantinople.
positions/byzantine-iconoclasm/responses: Iconoclasts held that Hieria was the true seventh ecumenical council and that the imperial church had the duty to reform worship.
positions/byzantine-iconoclasm/consequen: Destruction of much early Byzantine religious art (surviving icons are mainly from Sinai and Rome).
Strengthened monastic resistance and Rome's estrangement from Byzantium; Rome turned towards the Franks.
A precedent cited (and contrasted) in Reformation image debates.
positions/reformed-aniconism/oneLine: Images of God, Christ and the saints have no place in worship; the second commandment forbids them, God is to be known through the preached Word and the sacraments, and church buildings should be cleared of idols.
positions/reformed-aniconism/coreClaims/: The second commandment is a distinct commandment forbidding images in worship.
God wills to be known through his Word, not through ‘dumb images’ (Heidelberg Catechism Q. 98).
Images of Christ are improper because his divinity cannot be depicted and his humanity must not be separated from it.
Removing images restores true spiritual worship (John 4:24).
positions/reformed-aniconism/origin: Andreas Karlstadt's ‘On the Removal of Images’ (Wittenberg, 1522); Zwingli's Zürich (images removed 1524); Calvin (Institutes 1.11); English Edwardian injunctions (1547–8); the Dutch ‘Beeldenstorm’ (1566); Heidelberg Catechism (1563) Q. 96–98; Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 109.
positions/reformed-aniconism/strongestAr: It obeys a plain divine command.
It mirrors Old Testament reforms (Hezekiah breaking the bronze serpent when it became an idol, 2 Kings 18:4).
It focuses worship on the Word and the sacraments, avoiding superstition.
positions/reformed-aniconism/strongestOb: Lutherans (Luther, Invocavit sermons 1522) argued images are adiaphora and that compulsory destruction is legalism.
Orthodox and Catholics: it implicitly denies the incarnation's significance for matter and art.
It involved mob violence and the destruction of irreplaceable art.
positions/reformed-aniconism/responses/0: Reformed theologians distinguish images in worship (forbidden) from art in general (permitted).
positions/reformed-aniconism/responses/1: Calvin argued that the early church's first centuries were without images in worship.
positions/reformed-aniconism/consequence: Whitewashed churches and plain meeting-houses in Reformed lands; wordcentred architecture.
Iconoclastic riots (Netherlands 1566; Scotland 1559) and lasting confessional differences in church art.
Shaped Protestant missionary practice of avoiding images.
positions/marian-coredemption/name: Marian co-redemption and mediation of all graces
positions/marian-coredemption/oneLine: Mary cooperated uniquely with Christ in the work of redemption — by her consent, her suffering at the cross and her ongoing intercession — so that she may be called Co-redemptrix and Mediatrix of all graces, always subordinate to Christ.
positions/marian-coredemption/coreClaims: Mary's ‘fiat’ (Luke 1:38) was a free cooperation necessary to the incarnation.
Her compassion at the cross (Luke 2:35; John 19:25) united her to Christ's sacrifice in a unique way.
All graces are distributed through her intercession (Mediatrix).
The prefix ‘co-’ (from Latin cum, ‘with’) means cooperation, not equality.
positions/marian-coredemption/origin: Medieval devotion (Arnold of Chartres, Bernardine of Siena); ‘Coredemptrix’ in some 17th–20th-century writings and occasional papal usage (Pius XI); Louis de Montfort's True Devotion (c. 1712); the Vox Populi Mariae Mediatrici movement (1990s) petitioned for a dogma; Vatican II (Lumen Gentium 60–62) avoided the title; the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith's note Mater Populi Fidelis (2025) judged ‘Co-redemptrix’ inappropriate.
positions/marian-coredemption/strongestA: It expresses the real cooperation of a creature in salvation, analogous to Paul's ‘filling up what is lacking in Christ's afflictions’ (Colossians 1:24).
It has deep roots in Catholic devotion and was used occasionally by popes (John Paul II used ‘Co-redemptrix’ a handful of times).
positions/marian-coredemption/strongestO: It obscures Christ's unique redemption and is easily misunderstood, damaging ecumenism (as Cardinal Ratzinger and the 2025 doctrinal note argued).
No basis in Scripture or the early Fathers for Mary as mediator of all graces.
Protestants and Orthodox see it as confirming their fears about Marian excess.
positions/marian-coredemption/responses/: Advocates insist that all of Mary's role is derived from and dependent on Christ, as Lumen Gentium 62 affirms of ‘subordinate’ mediation.
positions/marian-coredemption/consequenc: Petitions for a fifth Marian dogma were not granted; the Vatican's 2025 note discouraged the title.
A recurring point of ecumenical sensitivity.
positions/great-commission-evangelism/al: Evangelization of the world in this generation
positions/great-commission-evangelism/on: The church’s central mission is to proclaim Christ to every people so that they may repent, believe and be gathered into churches; this task remains binding on every generation and is urgent because people are lost without Christ.
positions/great-commission-evangelism/co: The Great Commission binds the church until the end of the age (Matt 28:20).
Humanity is lost apart from Christ, so evangelism has priority, though not exclusivity, in the church’s mission.
Every "people group" (ethnos) must be reached; the gospel must be preached in all the world before the end (Matt 24:14).
Mission is the task of every believer, organised through voluntary societies and churches.
positions/great-commission-evangelism/or: Practised from the apostles onward; given modern Protestant form by William Carey’s Enquiry (1792) and the missionary societies; amplified by Hudson Taylor, the Student Volunteer Movement ("the evangelization of the world in this generation", 1886), Edinburgh 1910, Lausanne 1974 (which said evangelism is primary) and Ralph Winter’s "unreached people groups" (1974).
positions/great-commission-evangelism/st: It takes the risen Christ’s last command at face value.
If salvation is through faith in Christ, love for neighbours requires telling them.
Its fruit is visible in the growth of churches in Korea, Africa, Latin America and among unreached peoples.
Critics argue it reduces mission to verbal proclamation and neglects justice and service (an objection pressed by Latin American evangelicals at Lausanne).
Its alliance with Western power and culture produced paternalism and cultural imperialism.
Pluralists and many in other religions see conversion efforts as disrespectful or as proselytism.
positions/great-commission-evangelism/re: Defenders reply that evangelism and social care go together, but that only the gospel addresses humanity’s deepest need of reconciliation with God (Lausanne Covenant 6).
They point out that most missionaries today come from the Global South and that converts often embraced Christianity against colonial interests.
positions/great-commission-evangelism/co: The modern missionary movement and the global spread of Protestantism.
Bible translation into over 700 complete languages.
Strategies such as people-group research, the 10/40 Window and church-planting movements.
positions/jesuit-accommodation/oneLine: Missionaries should adapt to the language, dress, manners and intellectual traditions of a people, treating civil customs such as ancestral rites as compatible with Christianity, and presenting the gospel as the fulfilment of their best wisdom.
positions/jesuit-accommodation/coreClaim: Grace perfects nature: truths in Confucian, Hindu and other traditions can be preparation for the gospel.
Missionaries should become "all things to all men", adopting local dress, language and etiquette.
Rites honouring ancestors and Confucius are civil and familial, not idolatrous worship.
Indigenous terms (Tian, Shangdi) can name the true God.
Conversion of elites can open whole societies to the faith.
positions/jesuit-accommodation/origin: Developed by Alessandro Valignano for Japan (1579), practised by Matteo Ricci in China (in Beijing from 1601) and Roberto de Nobili in India (from 1606); condemned in the Chinese Rites (1704–1742) and Malabar Rites (1704–1744) controversies; rehabilitated in 1939 and echoed by Vatican II.
positions/jesuit-accommodation/strongest: Paul at Athens quoted pagan poets and built on the "unknown god".
It won respected converts among Chinese literati and built a lasting Chinese Catholic community.
Treating filial piety as idolatry made conversion appear to require betraying one’s family and nation.
Dominicans and Franciscans argued that ancestral rites included sacrifice and prayers to spirits, so tolerating them was syncretism.
Accepting caste distinctions in India (de Nobili) seemed to contradict Christian equality.
Elite-focused strategy depended on imperial favour and collapsed when it was withdrawn.
positions/jesuit-accommodation/responses: Defenders noted that the Kangxi Emperor himself declared the rites civil (1700) and that Rome reversed its ban in 1939.
They argued that de Nobili distinguished social customs from religious ones and that later accommodation could correct abuses.
positions/jesuit-accommodation/consequen: Chinese Rites controversy and the decline of the Qing-era mission.
Suppression of the Jesuits (1773) was hastened by these disputes.
positions/inculturation-contextualizatio: Inculturation and contextualisation
Inculturation (Catholic term)
Contextualisation (Protestant term)
Indigenisation
Localisation

The gospel must be expressed through each culture’s language, symbols, music, thought-forms and social realities, so that Christ becomes at home among every people while also transforming their cultures.
The incarnation is the model: the Word took flesh in a particular culture.
No culture, including Western Christian culture, is normative; all are both affirmed and judged by the gospel.
Local theologies arise from the meeting of Scripture and context (Bevans’ "models of contextual theology").
Pre-Christian religious heritage can be a preparation for the gospel (Bediako, Mbiti).
Critical contextualisation tests customs by Scripture to avoid syncretism (Paul Hiebert).
John 1:14
Acts 15
1 Corinthians 9:19–23
Revelation 21:24–26

The term "contextualization" was coined by Shoki Coe and Aharon Sapsezian in the Theological Education Fund (1972); "inculturation" was popularised by Jesuit superior Pedro Arrupe (1978) and John Paul II (Catechesi Tradendae, 1979) following Evangelii Nuntiandi (1975). Roots in early Syriac, Ethiopian and Celtic Christianity and in Jesuit accommodation.

Pedro Arrupe

Aloysius Pieris
The Jerusalem council refused to impose Jewish culture on Gentile believers (Acts 15).
Christianity has always been translated into new cultures (Greek, Latin, Syriac, Slavic), so the principle is ancient.
Faith that remains foreign stays shallow; indigenous expression produces deep and lasting churches.
Critics warn of syncretism, when culture rather than Scripture sets the agenda (e.g. accommodation to ancestor veneration or caste).
Some argue that "context" can be used to relativise doctrine and ethics (debates in the Anglican Communion).
Postcolonial critics note that outsiders often decide what counts as authentic local culture.
Proponents distinguish critical contextualisation (Scripture judges culture) from uncritical accommodation.
They argue that every theology, including Western theology, is contextual, so the real choice is between conscious and unconscious contextualisation.
African, Asian and Latin American theologies; local music and art in worship.
Zaire Use of the Roman Rite (1988) and Indian Christian ashrams.
Debates over insider movements among Muslim-background believers.
